full_judgment: 14. Mr Md Abul Bashar, the learned Advocate appearing as State Defence Lawyer on behalf of absconding convict Abdul Jabbar Lablu alias Labu, adopts the submissions made on behalf of condemned prisoner Salauddin @ Tipu. In addition, he points out that the place of occurrence, according to the first information report, was the Rickshaw Sramik Union Office, whereas in the charge the place of occurrence has been noted as the torture chamber adjacent to accused Taher's house and, therefore, the charge is defective. He also submits that there is a misjoinder of charge, inasmuch as there ought to have been individual charge against each individual accused person. The learned Advocate points out that the prosecution's explanation regarding the delay in lodging the first information report cannot be accepted where the delay has been for one year and two months and the police station is only 200 yards away from the place of occurrence. He submits that when such an occurrence took place there must have been information to the police and the police must have come to the place of occurrence having recorded a diary, but the prosecution withheld the real story. The learned Advocate further points out that the surathal report does not name any accused persons, although by that time the names of the assailants had been known by the informant, as he had heard about the occurrence from the victim himself and had been told the names of the accused persons. The learned Advocate submits that the prosecution must prove the case with regard to place, time and manner of occurrence and there must be a clear finding of the Court in this regard, as was held in the case of Abdul Karim vs States another, 1981 BLD (AD) 200. He also refers to Alkas Mia and others vs State; 25 DLR 398 and submits that non-examination of independent witnesses, when they would naturally have been available, should lead to an adverse inference being drawn against the prosecution under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. He submits that the place of occurrence being a market place there would have been permanent shop owners who would have been disinterested and competent witnesses, but they were not examined. He refers to Habibullah and others vs State, 21 DLR (SC) 88 and submits that, where the first information report is belated, it is unworthy of credit and that statements of witnesses made shortly after the occurrence would carry more weight.
